===== 202

Change 202 · interpreter.md, “What walk checks”A valid nested pair of a generic trait’s functional methods stops the run when the program first makes an extending object
New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in
interpreter.md, “What walk checks”, line 68, the first of walk’s departures under its first refusal, on two functional methods of a generic trait or object: its third sentence; the first two did not change
At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So [-such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with “Cannot find definition for method”-]{+where the two declared domains lie one inside the other, a valid pair stops the run when the program first makes the extending object at its static arguments, as H[\ZZ32\]() for object H[\S\]() extends Holds[\S\]: 'at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types'+} (ledger row 780).

Why. Not a new rule: a departure of walk, as the batch changed it. The bullet said that walk loads such a pair of functional methods that breaks the rules, and that a call can fail with “Cannot find definition for method” (row 780). That has been false since climb batch 36, which made walk keep two generic dotted methods that differ in their bounds as two overloads (change 190). Now, where the two declared domains lie one inside the other, walk checks the pair when the program first makes an object that extends the trait, and refuses a valid pair there: ‘at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types’. A worker who read the old text would have looked for a failure at a call. The bullet’s first two sentences stay, as the orientation’s judge asked. The landing changed the words of the curator’s decision P-45 to match, and the decision itself is unchanged. After the cold read, one fix. The first wording said that the refusal comes “when walk first makes an instance of an object that extends the trait”. That could mean making the object when the program runs, or filling in its static arguments at load, so a worker could not tell whether a test expects a refusal at load or a stop during the run. The text now says that the run stops when the program first makes the extending object at its static arguments, and gives the example of the row’s test: H[\ZZ32\]() for object H[\S\]() extends Holds[\S\]. The skill writer checked this against that test and walk’s code. The skill writer left one point to the coordinator: the kept sentence, that walk compares the methods at each call, now stands beside the stop when the object is made, and a reader may find the two hard to reconcile. Rewriting it would change what the rule means.

===== 136

Change 136 · compiler.md, “The checker’s gaps”The checker no longer breaks a tie by what the JVM compiled before, so the bullet on it is cut
No new text: what this item added is cut; struck through, the cut text
compiler.md, “The checker’s gaps”, line 178 before climb batch 36, the fourth bullet, which this item added after the bullet of change 175, now cut whole
[-A tie: where two generic candidates fit a call equally, the checker sorts the candidates and keeps the first. The sort's order varies with what the same JVM compiled before. So the call's static type, or a crash, 'V is not in the kind env', can change with the order of the suite (ledger rows 499, 1046, 1047). If a compiled test passes alone and fails in the suite, look for such a tie first.-]

Why. Not a new rule: a gap of the checker that climb batch 31’s gate met. The batch added a compiled test whose one assertion was the checker’s crash ‘V is not in the kind env’, on a call that two generic candidates fit equally (row 1046). Alone, the compile crashed as the test expected. In the gate’s suite it did not, and the gate was red on that test alone, so the gate’s repair took the test out of the gated tests. The cause: where two generic candidates tie, the checker sorts them and keeps the first, and the sort’s order varies with what the same JVM compiled before. So a call’s static type, or the crash, can change with the order of the suite (rows 499, 1046 and 1047). The part had no sentence on it, so a worker whose test passes alone and fails in the suite would have searched its own change. After the cold read, two fixes. The first wording said that the checker “keeps the head of its sort”, which named no sort: the text now says that it sorts the candidates and keeps the first. And the bullet gave no action: it now says to look for such a tie first. The cold read also proposed “make one candidate more specific than the other”. The skill writer did not add it, since no record shows that it works. Nor did it add a rule on how to record such a defect in a test, since that would change the meaning of tests-writing.md, which the coordinator judges first.
Why, climb batch 36. Not a new rule: a gap that the batch fixed. The bullet said that where two generic declarations fit a call equally, the checker sorts them and keeps the first, in an order that varies with what the same JVM compiled before. So a compiled test could pass alone and fail in its suite (rows 499, 1046 and 1047), and the bullet told a worker to look for such a tie first. Climb batch 36 made the checker choose among a call’s declarations by their signatures as declared, in the order of their places in the program, and refuse a tie that the rules leave. Rows 1046 and 1047 are fixed, and row 499 now holds only a defect of the compiled dispatch. So a call’s type no longer changes with the order of the suite, and the bullet is gone. Nothing of this item stands in the skill now. One case is left: among a program’s own declarations, the checker keeps the first by place of a tie that no rule decides (row 1136). The skill writer added no sentence for it, since whether the place may decide was then a question for the curator. The curator’s decision P-181, written at 09:02 UTC after the landing, settles it: the order of declarations never decides a call; a rule of the language decides it, or the call is a static error. The cold read asked whether the cut leaves a worker whose compiled test passes alone and fails in its suite with no first place to look. The skill writer kept the cut, since the checker’s choice no longer depends on what the JVM compiled before.

revival-changes.md, “Dispatch and overloading”, line 15, the rule that walk chooses by declared parameter types, whole: the three sentences that this item added after its third, now cut; the rest did not change
Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations. It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. [-In a departure, where two generic dotted methods of one name and parameter count differ only in their static parameters' bounds, walk drops one at load. Every call then runs the other, or stops where the argument is outside its bound. So with tk[\U extends Number\](y: U) declared before tk[\U extends ZZ32\](y: U), a call on a ZZ32 runs the first (row 1125).-] It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with “Cannot unify”.

Why. Not a new rule: a departure of walk that the batch found. The rule says that walk chooses among overloads by their declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations. Climb batch 35b made walk run two generic dotted methods of one name that differ in their number of parameters (change 138). Its checks then found a case beside it where the rule does not hold: of two generic dotted methods of one name and one number of parameters that differ only in the bounds of their static parameters, walk drops one at load (row 1125). Every call then runs the other, also where the dropped one is more specific, or stops where the argument is outside the kept one’s bound. So with tk[\U extends Number\](y: U) declared before tk[\U extends ZZ32\](y: U), a call on a ZZ32 runs the first, where the rule runs the second. The rule stays, and three new sentences name the departure, with its ledger row. They give no way round it: by the curator’s decision P-180, a defect is fixed, not taught, and its fix waits for the coordinator’s plan. The skill writer named a decision not taken: to soften “never” in the rule’s heading in place of naming the departure. The landing changed the words of F-26 and F-253, two FACTS entries on walk’s choice, to name this exception. After the cold read, one fix. The first wording said that walk “keeps the first that it meets”. That named no order, right after a heading that says the order does not count, and it did not say whether the other method ever runs, or which bounds differ. The text now says that walk drops one at load, and that every call runs the other or stops outside its bound, and it gives the example of the ledger row’s test. It does not say which one walk keeps in general: walk keeps the one that its environment meets first, and the skill writer could not confirm that this is the order in the source, so the order shows only in the example. The cold read also asked for a step to avoid the trap, such as two names for the two methods. The skill writer left it out, by P-180.
Why, climb batch 36. Not a new rule: a departure that the batch fixed. The three sentences said that, of two generic dotted methods of one name and parameter count that differ only in their static parameters’ bounds, walk drops one at load, so that every call runs the other (row 1125). Climb batch 36 made walk keep both, each as an overload of its own, and choose between them by their declared domains (F-405). So the rule that walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations, now holds for them too, and the three sentences are gone. A worker who read them would have expected the wrong method to run. The landing changed the words of F-26 and F-253, two FACTS entries on walk’s choice, to match. The orientation update made the cut, and its judge said to install it. Nothing of this item stands in the skill now. The cold read found nothing to fix here.

Change 91 · revival-changes.md, “Dispatch and overloading”The example of walk’s load check on two functional methods of a generic trait, cut since the batch made it false

revival-changes.md, “Dispatch and overloading”, line 17, the rule that walk’s load check is not the verdict, its last sentence, now cut whole; the rest did not change
[-For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains only at a call (row 780).-]

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule’s meaning: a sentence that read two ways. It said that walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object “on their declared domains only at a call”. “Only” could go with “declared domains” or with “at a call”. The sentence now says “at each call, not at load”, as interpreter.md, “What walk checks”, states the case. The orientation update made the change, and its judge checked it against that part and the ledger row and said to install it.
Why, climb batch 36. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule’s meaning: an example that the batch made false, cut. The rule says that walk’s load check is not the verdict of these rules. Its example said that walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object at each call, not at load (row 780). Climb batch 36 changed what walk does with such a pair. Where their declared domains lie one inside the other, walk now refuses a valid pair when the program first makes an object that extends the trait, not at a call (change 202). The orientation update first rewrote the example to say so. Its own cold read found that the new wording used a term that the part does not define, and that the example gave a worker no action. So the update cut the example, and its judge said to install the cut. The rule still sends a worker to interpreter.md, “What walk checks”, which holds the case. Against the text before this item, the sentence is cut whole, and nothing of this item stands in the skill now.
